note: Sources: NASA Science InSight mission overview and JPL release resources.

facts.text: InSight touched down on the smooth, flat plains of Elysium Planitia on Mars on November 26, 2018.
InSight was designed to study the deep interior of Mars — its crust, mantle, and core — using seismic, heat flow, and rotation experiments.
Two briefcase-sized CubeSats, MarCO-A and MarCO-B, flew past Mars during InSight's landing to relay telemetry in near real time.
facts.sourceName: NASA Science: Mars Cube One (challenge resource)

facts.text: InSight used its robotic arm to place the SEIS seismometer directly onto the Martian ground, protected by a Wind and Thermal Shield dome.
SEIS recorded more than 1,300 seismic events on Mars, including its largest detected quake of magnitude 5 on May 4, 2022.
The HP3 heat flow probe, nicknamed the Mole, could not reach its planned 5-meter depth due to unexpected soil friction and cohesion.
The RISE experiment used radio tracking from Earth to measure Mars' wobble, helping constrain the size of its large liquid iron-rich core.
Over four years, Martian dust accumulated on InSight's solar panels, gradually cutting electrical power output.
InSight made its final communication with Earth on December 15, 2022, and NASA formally retired the mission on December 21, 2022.
